*Note that all times shown here use ET.*

```{r program, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
program_table <- read.delim("static/program.tsv")[, -1]
link_title <- function(titles) {
    sapply(1:length(titles), function(i) {
        title <- titles[i]
        if (title %in% c("Welcome", "Break", "Wrap up")) {
            return(title)
        }
        title <- paste0(c("[", title, "]", "(#session", i, ")"), collapse = "")
        title
    })
}

program_table <- program_table %>% mutate(Title = link_title(Title))

knitr::kable(program_table, format = "html") %>%
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c(
        "striped", "hover",
        "condensed", "responsive"
    )) %>%
    column_spec(1, width = "5em") %>%
    column_spec(2, width = "5em")
```

### Latent CMV is Associated with Putative CMV-specific Clonal Expansion in Th1 and GZMK⁺ CD8⁺ T Cells {#session2}

<strong>Titas Grabauskas</strong><sup>1,2,‡</sup>, 
Luke Trinity<sup>1,‡</sup>, Chris P. Verschoor<sup>3,4</sup>, 
Radu Marches<sup>1</sup>, Asa Thibodeau<sup>1</sup>, Djamel Nehar-Belaid<sup>1</sup>,

Cathleen Colon-Emeric<sup>5</sup>, Heather E. Whitson<sup>5</sup>, Silke Paust<sup>1</sup>, 
Adolfo García-Sastre<sup>6-11</sup>, Gur Yaari<sup>12</sup>, 
Jacques Banchereau<sup>1,13,\*</sup>, George A. Kuchel<sup>2,14,\*</sup>, and Duygu Ucar<sup>1,15,\*</sup>

<sup>\*</sup>Corresponding authors: duygu.ucar@jax.org, jacques.banchereau@gmail.com, kuchel@uchc.edu  

<div class="abstract-box">
<strong>Abstract:</strong>

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a common herpesvirus that establishes lifelong latency and becomes increasingly prevalent 
with age. While CMV-associated effects on CD4+/CD8+ TEMRA and NK cells are well established, the impact on other 
immune populations and T cell clonal expansion remain poorly defined. Here, we used single-cell RNA-sequencing 
and flow cytometry to profile peripheral blood mononuclear cells from healthy older adults (median age: 73), 
stratified by CMV serostatus with comparable age, sex, BMI, and frailty. Systems-level characterization identified 
novel CMV-associated changes in cell frequencies: increase in GZMK⁺ CD8⁺ T and atypical B cells, and reduction in 
CD56dim NK cells. We also validated these observations in an independent younger adult cohort. To infer CMV 
serostatus in single-cell datasets lacking serological data, we developed CMVerify, a machine learning model that 
predicts CMV serostatus with 97% accuracy (97% sensitivity; 98% specificity). Applying CMVerify and 
Immcantation’s Alakazam to a public single-cell dataset with TCR sequencing (and no CMV serology data) revealed 
reduced TCR clonal diversity in CMV-seropositive individuals across CD4+/CD8+ TEMRAs, GZMK⁺ CD8⁺ T, and Th1 cells. 
Importantly, we show that putatively expanded CMV-specific clones within these subsets drive the reduction in TCR 
clonal diversity. Our results establish CMV as a key driver of immune heterogeneity in both younger and older adults, 
describe novel associations, and present a tool to effectively infer CMV serostatus from single-cell data. 
</div>

### Nucleotide Context Models Outperform Protein Language Models For Predicting Antibody Affinity Maturation {#session3}

Mackenzie M. Johnson<sup>1</sup>, Kevin Sung<sup>1</sup>, Hugh K. Haddox<sup>1</sup>, 
Ashni A. Vora<sup>2</sup>, Tatsuya Araki<sup>2</sup>, Gabriel Victora<sup>2</sup>, 
Yun S. Song<sup>4,5</sup>, Julia Fukuyama<sup>6</sup>, Frederick A. Matsen IV<sup>1,3,7,8,\*</sup> 

<sup>1</sup>Computational Biology Program, Fred Hutch Cancer Center; 
<sup>2</sup>Laboratory of Lymphocyte Dynamics, The Rockefeller University; 
<sup>3</sup>Howard Hughes Medical Instititute; 
<sup>4</sup>Computer Science Division, University of California, Berkeley; 
<sup>5</sup>Department of Statistics, University of California, Berkeley; 
<sup>6</sup>Department of Statistics, Indiana University, Bloomington; 
<sup>7</sup>Department of Genome Sciences, University of Washington; 
<sup>8</sup>Department of Statistics, University of Washington 

<sup>\*</sup>Corresponding author 

<div class="abstract-box">
<strong>Abstract:</strong>
Antibodies play a crucial role in adaptive immunity. They develop as B cell receptors (BCRs) that are 
expressed on the surfaces of B cells. BCRs are refined through affinity maturation, a process of somatic 
hypermutation (SHM) and natural selection, to improve binding to an antigen. Computational models of 
affinity maturation have developed from two main perspectives: molecular evolution and language modeling. 
The molecular evolution perspective focuses on nucleotide sequence context to describe mutation and 
selection; the language modeling perspective involves learning patterns from large data sets of protein 
sequences. We compared models from both perspectives on their ability to predict the course of antibody 
affinity maturation along phylogenetic trees of BCR sequences. This included models of SHM – such as 
the S5F model, models of SHM combined with an estimate of selection, and protein language models AbLang2 
and ESM-1v. We evaluated models on large human BCR repertoire data sets, as well as an antigen-specific 
mouse experiment with a pre-rearranged cognate naive antibody. We demonstrated that precise modeling 
of SHM, which requires the nucleotide context, provides a substantial amount of predictive power 
for predicting the course of affinity maturation. Notably, a simple nucleotide-based convolutional 
neural network modeling SHM outperformed state-of-the-art protein language models, including one trained 
exclusively on antibody sequences. Furthermore, incorporating estimates of selection based on a custom 
deep mutational scanning experiment brought only modest improvement in predictive power. To support 
further research, we introduce EPAM (Evaluating Predictions of Affinity Maturation), a benchmarking 
framework to integrate evolutionary principles with advances in language modeling. 
</div>

<strong>Associated publications:</strong>
